Methods for interacting systems

Robust & efficient
spatiotemporal graph learning

How do we learn from networks that evolve, contain noise, and have missing observations? I develop adaptive graph augmentation, contrastive learning, and efficient temporal architectures to capture useful structure at scale.

Knowledge-guided scientific AI

Biological discovery &
precision medicine

How can scientific knowledge improve prediction when data are limited? I investigate models that adapt quantum, geometric, biological, and anatomical priors, with a current focus on forecasting regional tau changes in Alzheimer’s disease using longitudinal PET.

02 / About me

A foundation in graph learning.
A focus on scientific discovery.

I develop domain-knowledge-adaptive AI: models that combine relationships in data with scientific knowledge to make predictions under noise, limited observations, and computational constraints.

I am a Postdoctoral Associate at Yale University, working with Georges El Fakhri, Jingsong Ouyang, and Xiaofeng Liu. I received my Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of Hong Kong, advised by Siu-Ming Yiu, and was a visiting postdoctoral researcher at the University of Cambridge with Pietro Liò.

01 / Structure

Represent interactions

Use graphs to preserve dependencies and distinct types of relationships between entities.

02 / Robustness

Adapt to imperfect data

Learn useful representations through adaptive augmentation and contrastive objectives.

03 / Knowledge

Use scientific priors

Adapt domain knowledge to the task and evaluate where it helps—and where it fails.

04 / Efficiency

Make prediction practical

Reduce computational cost through knowledge distillation and hierarchical temporal modeling.

Looking ahead

An independent
research agenda.

I aim to build a research group developing reusable algorithms and rigorous benchmarks for interacting systems. In biomedicine, my next steps are to evaluate longitudinal imaging forecasts across cohorts and investigate how imaging and genomic information can support more individualized models of disease progression.
